q1: SELECT b1.name AS bar1, b2.name AS bar2 FROM bar AS b1, bar AS b2 WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT s1.beer FROM serves AS s1 WHERE s1.bar = b1.name AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM serves AS s2 WHERE s2.bar = b2.name AND s2.beer = s1.beer)) AND EXISTS(SELECT s2.beer FROM serves AS s2 WHERE s2.bar = b2.name AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM serves AS s1 WHERE s1.bar = b1.name AND s1.beer = s2.beer))
q2: SELECT a.bar, b.bar FROM serves AS a LEFT OUTER JOIN serves AS b ON a.bar <> b.bar AND a.beer = b.beer

q2_prompt_sql: SELECT a.bar, b.bar FROM serves AS a LEFT OUTER JOIN serves AS b ON a.bar <> b.bar AND a.beer = b.beer
counterexample: INSERT INTO Bar (name, address) VALUES ('A', 'addressA'), ('B', 'addressB'); INSERT INTO Beer (name, brewer) VALUES ('X', 'brewerX'), ('Y', 'brewerY'); INSERT INTO Serves (bar, beer, price) VALUES ('A', 'X', 1.00), ('B', 'Y', 1.00);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because Q1 checks for bars that serve a unique beer (no other bar serves the same beer) and another bar that does not serve that beer, while Q2 checks for all pairs of bars that serve the same beer.
counterexample_dsp: A test case where Bar A serves beer X and Bar B serves beer Y, and no other bar serves beer X or Y. This triggers the difference because Q1 will return (A, B) and (B, A) as the bars that satisfy the conditions, while Q2 will return all pairs of bars that serve the same beer, which in this case is (A, B) and (B, A).
